title: Revenue Growth Management in CPG
summary: Revenue growth management in CPG: the five levers, why most RGM programs stall on data rather than strategy, and what has to exist before it works.
body_markdown:
Revenue growth management is the practice of treating pricing, promotion, product mix, pack architecture, and trade investment as one connected system rather than five decisions made by different people at different times. The premise is that those levers interact, and optimizing any one alone moves the others in ways nobody accounted for.


That premise is correct, and it is also why most RGM programs stall. The strategy is not the hard part. The hard part is that the five levers sit in five systems with five owners and no shared measurement, and a program that does not fix that first produces a framework instead of a result.


## Key takeaways


- RGM is five levers treated as one system: price, promotion, pack architecture, mix, and trade investment.
- The most common failure is organizational, not analytical. Different owners, different data, no shared baseline.
- Start with the promotion lever. It is the largest, the most measurable, and usually the most wasteful.
- Without a defensible baseline method, every RGM number is contested and the program dies in the debate.


## The five revenue growth management levers


Lever The question Usual owner


Price Where should everyday shelf price sit, per item per retailer Finance or marketing


Promotion Which offers, how deep, how often, and what did they return Sales and trade


Pack architecture Which sizes at which price points, and how they ladder Marketing and R&D


Mix Which items and channels get the push Sales leadership


Trade investment How the fund is allocated across accounts and tactics Sales finance


Read the third column. Those are five different people, often in three different functions, each measured on something different. A price increase that improves margin can wreck a volume target; a promotion that hits a volume number can destroy the margin the price move earned. RGM as a discipline exists to make that trade-off explicit rather than accidental, and it only works if one number is agreed.


## Net revenue management is the same discipline


Net revenue management, or NRM, names these same five levers in a different house style, and a company running one is not missing the other. The two terms carry different emphasis rather than different content. RGM is usually written from the growth side, starting at the levers and asking what each can add. NRM is usually written from the gross-to-net side, starting at list price and walking down through discounts, allowances, promotion, and deductions to the revenue actually collected. Same arithmetic, opposite direction of travel.


Which word your organization uses tends to follow who owns the program. Where it sits in commercial finance you will hear NRM and the first slide will be a gross-to-net waterfall. Where it sits in sales or marketing you will hear RGM and the first slide will be the five levers. The difference is small and it is not nothing: an NRM framing surfaces the deduction gap early, because settled deductions are a line in the walk, while an RGM framing can run two quarters on planned trade cost before anyone notices the 20 percent difference described below.


## Why RGM programs stall


- No shared baseline. Sales measures promotion lift one way, finance another, and neither result is accepted by the other. Every meeting becomes a methodology argument.
- Planned rather than actual trade cost. Deductions land differently from what was planned, sometimes by 20 percent or more, and an RGM model built on planned spend is a forecast reporting itself as a result.
- Elasticity used at the wrong grain. One brand-level elasticity applied to every item and retailer will recommend price moves that are wrong nearly everywhere.
- Distribution not held constant. A price move during a distribution change reads as an elasticity result and is not.
- The tool arrives before the data. A platform sitting on inconsistent inputs produces confident recommendations nobody trusts, which is worse than no platform.


## Start with promotion


For most mid-size CPG brands, trade is the largest line after cost of goods and the one with the most obvious waste. It is also the most measurable, which makes it the right place to earn the credibility the rest of the program needs.


The sequence that works: build one baseline method everyone agrees to, re-cost the last four quarters of promotions using actual deductions, rank them by contribution rather than by volume, and stop the bottom decile. That is a concrete result inside a quarter, and it funds the argument for the harder levers.


A worked example. A brand ran 46 promoted events across three retailers in a year. Re-costed with actual deductions and measured against a consistent baseline, 11 events produced negative contribution, and those 11 consumed 22 percent of the trade budget. Nine of them were repeat events that had run quarterly for years because nobody had ever computed them individually. Stopping seven of the eleven returned about $310,000 to the fund with no volume consequence outside a rounding error.


## What has to exist before RGM works


- Item-level price, promotion, and distribution history at a consistent grain across retailers.
- Actual deduction data joined to the promotion it belongs to, not just to the period.
- A single baseline method, written down, that both sales and finance have signed off on.
- Elasticity estimated per item per retailer, with base and promoted separated.


That list is unglamorous and it is the whole job. Brands that build it find the analysis straightforward; brands that skip it buy software and hold workshops. See[trade spend management](https://www.cpgscout.ai/blog/trade-spend-management) and[price elasticity in CPG](https://www.cpgscout.ai/learn/price-elasticity-in-cpg) for the two components that carry the most weight.


A closing note on sequencing, because it is where good RGM intentions usually die. The levers are connected, which tempts teams into launching all five at once so the interactions are captured. In practice that produces a program with five workstreams, no early result, and a credibility problem by month six. Run them in sequence, prove one, and use the proof to fund the next. The interactions are real and they can be handled by revisiting earlier decisions once the data layer exists, which is cheaper than stalling on all of them at the same time.


## How Scout fits


Scout supplies the layer the list above describes: price, promotion, distribution, and velocity at one grain across retailers, with deduction cost carried into the contribution line so promotion results reflect what was actually taken. Elasticity is computed per item per retailer with base and promoted separated, which is the input an RGM decision needs and the one most often approximated.


Scout is the analytics layer, not a TPM system. It does not manage promotion execution, hold contracts, or settle claims; it measures what those systems did and recommends what to do next.


## Frequently asked questions


What is revenue growth management?Treating price, promotion, pack architecture, mix, and trade investment as one connected system rather than as separate decisions, on the basis that the levers interact and optimizing one in isolation shifts the others.


Where should a brand start with RGM?Promotion. It is usually the largest controllable line, the most measurable, and the one with the most visible waste. A concrete result there funds the credibility the harder levers need.


Do I need an RGM platform?Not first. A platform sitting on inconsistent price, promotion, distribution, and deduction data produces confident recommendations nobody trusts. Fix the data grain and the baseline method before buying tooling.


Why do RGM programs fail?Most often for organizational reasons: five levers with five owners and no agreed measurement, so every result is contested. The analytical problems, mainly wrong-grain elasticity and planned rather than actual trade cost, follow from the same root.
